newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Saab Auto drives deeper into red in first half.
newsitem.headline: Saab Auto drives deeper into red in first half.

text.p: Saab Automobile AB drove deeper into the red in the first half year of 1997 and analysts Tuesday ruled out a U-turn before the launch of the Swedish carmaker's new model later this year.

Saab Auto, owned by Swedish investment group Investor AB and U.S. auto giant General Motors Corp., posted a pretax loss of 600 million crowns ($74.5 million) for the six-month period, against a loss of 428 million ($53 million) for the first half of last year.

Sales rose to 10.98 billion crowns ($1.36 billion) from 10.13 billion ($1.26 billion), while operating losses widened to 394 million crowns ($49 million) from 95 million ($12 million), depressing the operating margin to a negative 3.3 percent from a negative 0.9 percent.
"It's in line with expectations although it looks terrible," said Gustaf von Essen, analyst at Sweden's Carnegie stockbrokers.
Saab Chief Executive Robert Hendry blamed the deeper losses on costs of new products and marketing, and said this could continue for the rest of the year.

Saab Auto's loss of 1.24 billion crowns ($154 million) for the full-year 1996 was largely blamed on marketing costs, and the company warned that it expected earnings to remain depressed for at least another year.

"For the second half of 1997 we expect, as we have previously indicated, that ongoing product development and marketing initiatives will keep pressure on profitability," Hendry said in a statement accompanying the results.
"It was just as bad as expected and it will probably continue at about the same pace for the rest of the year," one analyst said.

Six-month sales volumes rose 3 percent to 50,800 cars, and Saab said it saw sharp sales increases in The Netherlands, up 37 percent, Britain, up 26 percent, Sweden, up 20 percent, and Germany, up 15 percent.

Analysts have said the future of the carmaker, which has only two models and has been beset by financial woes for most of the 1990s, hinges on the launch of its 9-5 model in September. They say they do not expect to see better figures from the company until next year. Saab has said it aims to sell 10,000 of the new 9-5 in 1997, accounting for 10 percent of total sales.
